name: GCSE Computer Science (AQA 8525)
material_vintage: AQA GCSE Computer Science (8525) specification, Version 1.2 (29 November 2022), the current version linked from aqa.org.uk/8525, itemised on 2026-09-27: every AQA content reference across subject content sections 3.1 Fundamentals of algorithms, 3.2 Programming, 3.3 Fundamentals of data representation, 3.4 Computer systems, 3.5 Fundamentals of computer networks, 3.6 Cyber security, 3.7 Relational databases and SQL, and 3.8 Ethical, legal and environmental impacts of digital technology. Assessment: two written papers, each 50% of the GCSE and linear (both sat at the end of the course) -- Paper 1 Computational thinking and problem-solving (2 hours, 90 marks, covering 3.1-3.2, a mix of multiple-choice, short-answer and longer programming/problem-solving questions) and Paper 2 Computing concepts (1 hour 45 minutes, 90 marks, covering 3.3-3.8, a mix of multiple-choice, short-answer, longer-answer, extended-response and SQL questions). Stage tests and the mock are original questions in AQA's style; every numerical answer (binary/hex conversions, storage and file-size calculations, Huffman/RLE compression, logic-gate truth tables) was computed and verified when this course was built. Python (AQA's own widely-used reference teaching language) is used for runnable code examples and code-output items; AQA's actual exams are set in AQA's own pseudo-code using only the constructs in 3.2, which this course also teaches and shows alongside the Python.
level_source: RQF Level 2 (GCSE, grades 1-9), per Ofqual's Register of Regulated Qualifications listing for this specification

learner_notices.text: AQA's own exams are set in AQA's pseudo-code, not Python. This course runs and checks code examples in Python (AQA's reference teaching language) so output can be verified for real, but make sure you can also read and write the equivalent AQA pseudo-code, since that is what Paper 1 actually uses.

This course uses AQA's decimal (SI) storage units throughout: 1 KB = 1,000 bytes, 1 MB = 1,000 KB, and so on -- not the older 1,024-based (binary) convention some other tools and operating systems display.
